items.stem: Describe the study by Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg (1988) and explain what it shows about culture and development.
items.answer: Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg (1988). Aim: to compare attachment types across cultures. Method: Meta-analysis of 32 Strange Situation studies from 8 countries (about 2,000 infants). Findings: secure attachment was most common everywhere; avoidant attachment was more common in West Germany and resistant attachment in Japan and Israel; intracultural variation was 1.5 times intercultural Link: culture and development.

items.stem: Describe the study by Kleinman (1982) and explain what it shows about culture and the expression of distress (somatisation).
items.answer: Kleinman (1982). Aim: to investigate how depression is expressed and diagnosed in Chinese culture. Method: Kleinman interviewed and assessed 100 patients diagnosed with neurasthenia at a psychiatric clinic in Hunan, China, using Western diagnostic criteria. Findings: most of the patients met Western criteria for major depression but reported mainly physical symptoms such as headaches, dizziness and fatigue Link: culture and the expression of distress (somatisation).

items.stem: With reference to Arnett (2008), explain how research has investigated sampling bias towards WEIRD populations.
items.answer: Arnett (2008). Aim: to examine the cultural composition of samples in leading American psychology journals. Method: Arnett analysed the samples reported in articles published in six APA journals between 2003 and 2007. Findings: about 96% of participants were from Western industrialised countries, which contain about 12% of the world's population; 68% were American Link: sampling bias towards WEIRD populations.

items.stem: "Mental disorders are identical in all cultures." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Core features of some disorders occur widely, but their expression, prevalence, interpretation and treatment vary considerably across cultures.
items.markingKey: Core features of some disorders occur widely, but their expression, prevalence, interpretation and treatment vary considerably across cultures. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Etic research is always biased and should never be used." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Etic research allows comparison and can identify universals; the problem is imposed etic, which can be reduced by combining it with emic research and careful translation.
items.markingKey: Etic research allows comparison and can identify universals; the problem is imposed etic, which can be reduced by combining it with emic research and careful translation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Most psychological findings cannot be generalised beyond WEIRD populations."
items.answer: Generalisation should not be assumed; each finding must be tested across cultures.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: 96% WEIRD samples (Arnett, 2008); WEIRD people are outliers (Henrich et al., 2010). Arguments against: some processes replicate widely (e.g. basic memory, emotion recognition); cross-cultural replications sometimes confirm findings. Supported judgement: Generalisation should not be assumed; each finding must be tested across cultures.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "emic approach"?
options: Studying behaviour from within a culture, using concepts and methods meaningful to its members
Applying concepts or measures developed in one culture to another as if they were universal
Judging other cultures by the standards of one's own culture, often seeing one's own as superior
A pattern of symptoms recognised mainly within a particular culture
items.answer: Studying behaviour from within a culture, using concepts and methods meaningful to its members
items.markingKey: A. "emic approach" is studying behaviour from within a culture, using concepts and methods meaningful to its members.

items.stem: Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan (2010) reported that susceptibility to the Müller-Lyer illusion was:
options: Absent among Americans
Identical across cultures
Much lower among San foragers of the Kalahari than among American undergraduates
Highest among San foragers
items.answer: Much lower among San foragers of the Kalahari than among American undergraduates
items.markingKey: C. Even basic perception varies across cultures.

To examine the cultural composition of samples in leading American psychology journals
To compare attachment types across cultures
To investigate how depression is expressed and diagnosed in Chinese culture

items.stem: Distinguish between cultural relativism and ethnocentrism.
items.answer: Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by one's own standards; cultural relativism interprets behaviour within its own cultural context.
items.markingKey: Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by one's own standards; cultural relativism interprets behaviour within its own cultural context. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how culture can influence cognition.
items.answer: Cultural practices and values shape attention and thinking styles - e.g. East Asian participants attend more to context and relationships (holistic) than American participants (analytic) (Masuda and Nisbett, 2001).

items.answer: WEIRD populations are psychologically unusual in many respects (e.g. individualism, analytic thinking, susceptibility to some illusions), so findings may not apply to most of the world's population.

items.stem: Explain the difference between cultural influences on relationships and cultural influences on health.
items.answer: Culture affects health through beliefs about illness, symptom expression and treatment; it affects relationships through norms about partner choice (arranged vs love marriage), family roles and communication.

items.answer: Carry out emic studies in each culture (interviews, observation) to find local meanings; identify common elements; build items from the shared elements; test for equivalence in each culture before comparing.

items.stem: Describe the study by Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan (2010) and explain what it shows about cultural bias in psychological research.

items.stem: Outline one way in which hikikomori in Japan shows culture and health.
items.answer: Some young adults in Japan withdraw completely from social life and stay in their rooms for months or years; the term hikikomori describes this pattern. items.stem: With reference to analytic and holistic attention in eye-tracking, explain how it illustrates culture and cognition.
items.answer: Chua, Boland and Nisbett (2005) tracked eye movements as Chinese and American students looked at photographs of objects on complex backgrounds; Chinese students made more fixations to the background. Eye-tracking provided an objective, etic measure supporting the holistic-analytic distinction

items.stem: Briefly describe a Western IQ test used in rural Kenya and explain what it reveals about cultural bias in research.
items.answer: A Western intelligence test is given to children in rural Kenya, who score lower than British children; local children are, however, highly skilled at identifying medicinal herbs (Sternberg et al., 2001). The test measures culturally specific knowledge and skills (imposed etic), so lower scores reflect test bias rather than lower intelligence

items.stem: With reference to Kulkofsky et al. (2011), explain how research has investigated culture and memory.
items.answer: Kulkofsky et al. (2011). Aim: to investigate whether the factors that predict flashbulb memories differ between cultures.
